content: William James, born on January 11, 1842, and passing on August 26, 1910, was a groundbreaking American psychologist and philosopher who was originally trained as a medical doctor. He authored influential works in the emerging field of psychology, educational psychology, the psychology of religious experience and mysticism, and the philosophy of pragmatism. He was the brother of the novelist Henry James and diarist Alice James. His family was known for its intellectual brilliance and eccentricity, particularly their connections to Swedenborgian theology and the literary and intellectual elites of their time. This intellectual environment has continued to attract the interest of historians, biographers, and critics. James received a diverse trans-Atlantic education, becoming fluent in German and French, and developed a cosmopolitan character. His family traveled to Europe multiple times during his childhood, a pattern that continued throughout his life, with James making a total of 15 European journeys. Initially inclined toward art, he apprenticed in the studio of William Morris Hunt in Newport, Rhode Island, but shifted to scientific studies at Harvard University’s Lawrence Scientific School in 1861. In his early adulthood, James suffered from various physical ailments, including issues with his eyes, back, stomach, and skin. He also experienced psychological symptoms diagnosed as neurasthenia, which included prolonged periods of depression and suicidal ideation. While two of his younger brothers, Garth Wilkinson and Robertson, fought in the Civil War, James and his siblings Henry and Alice experienced periods of invalidism. He transitioned to medical studies at Harvard Medical School in 1864. In 1865, he joined Louis Agassiz on a scientific expedition to the Amazon River but had to abandon the trip after eight months due to severe seasickness and a mild case of smallpox. His studies were further interrupted by illness in 1867, prompting him to travel to Germany in search of a cure, where he stayed until 1868. During this time, he began publishing reviews in literary periodicals such as the North American Review. He earned his M.D. degree in June 1869 but never practiced medicine. His soul-sickness was only resolved in 1872 after a period of intense philosophical searching. He married Alice Gibbens in 1878. James’s time in Germany was intellectually transformative, leading him to realize that his true interests lay in philosophy and psychology rather than medicine. Reflecting on this later in 1902, he wrote, I originally studied medicine in order to be a physiologist, but I drifted into psychology and philosophy from a sort of fatality. I never had any philosophic instruction, the first lecture on psychology I ever heard being the first I ever gave. James spent his entire academic career at Harvard University. He began as an instructor in physiology in 1873, later teaching anatomy, psychology, and philosophy. He became a full professor in 1885, held an endowed chair in psychology in 1889, and returned to philosophy in 1897. He retired as an emeritus professor of philosophy in 1907. His exposure to figures like Hermann Helmholtz in Germany and Pierre Janet in France influenced his introduction of scientific psychology courses at Harvard. He taught his first experimental psychology course during the 1875–1876 academic year. At Harvard, he participated in philosophical discussions with Charles Peirce, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and Chauncey Wright, which evolved into the Metaphysical Club, a group that significantly influenced American intellectual thought. After retiring in 1907, James continued to write and lecture, publishing works such as Pragmatism, A Pluralistic Universe, and The Meaning of Truth. However, his later years were marked by worsening cardiac pain, which intensified in 1909 while he worked on an unfinished philosophy text, later published posthumously as Some Problems in Philosophy. In 1910, he traveled to Europe for experimental treatments, which were unsuccessful. He returned home on August 18, and his heart failed on August 26, 1910, at his home in Chocorua, New Hampshire. James was a leading proponent of functionalism in psychology and pragmatism in philosophy. He was a founder of the American Society for Psychical Research and an advocate for alternative approaches to healing. He challenged his professional peers to maintain an open-minded approach to phenomena that might otherwise be dismissed. In an empirical study by Haggbloom et al., which used criteria such as citations and recognition, James was ranked as the 14th most eminent psychologist of the 20th century. James was a prolific writer, with a bibliography compiled by John McDermott spanning 47 pages. His monumental work, The Principles of Psychology (1890), consisted of 1,200 pages in two volumes and took 12 years to complete. He later published an abridged version, Psychology: The Briefer Course (1892), as a less rigorous introduction to the field. These works criticized both the English associationist school and the Hegelianism of his time, seeking instead to reconceptualize the human mind as inherently purposive and selective. In epistemology, James defined true beliefs as those that prove useful to the believer, asserting that truth is what works in the way of belief. This perspective, known as pragmatism, emphasizes the practical utility of truth to the individual. James also introduced the concept of radical empiricism, which posits that nature and experience cannot be fully separated for objective analysis, as the observer’s mind inevitably influences the outcome. James’s emphasis on diversity as the default human condition, in contrast to dualistic frameworks like Hegelian dialectics, has had a lasting influence on American culture, particularly among liberals. His concept of the stream of consciousness significantly impacted modernist literature and art. In his 1897 lecture The Will to Believe, James defended the right to justify belief in the absence of evidence, particularly in the context of religious faith. He argued that belief in God could be validated by the positive impact it has on one’s life. James made significant contributions to the philosophy of religion, particularly in his Gifford Lectures at the University of Edinburgh, which were later published as The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902). He argued that religious experience, rather than institutions, should be the primary focus of study, as institutions are merely the social descendants of individual genius. He also emphasized the value of intense, even pathological, experiences for understanding the mind, as they magnify normal processes. James investigated mystical experiences throughout his life, experimenting with substances like chloral hydrate, amyl nitrite, nitrous oxide, and peyote. He concluded that while mystical revelations hold truth for the individual experiencing them, they cannot claim universal validity without personal experience. James is also known for the James-Lange theory of emotion, developed independently of Carl Lange in the 1880s. This theory posits that emotions arise from the mind’s perception of physiological changes triggered by stimuli. For example, we do not fear a bear and then run; rather, we see the bear, run, and consequently feel fear. This perspective has significant implications for the philosophy of aesthetics. In the philosophy of history, James contributed to the debate on the role of individuals versus societal forces in shaping history. In his 1880 essay Great Men and Their Environment, he sided with the view that individuals, or heroes, drive historical change, though he expanded this concept beyond the political and military spheres to include cultural and intellectual contributions.
